newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end off highs after early rally - May 12.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end off highs after early rally - May 12.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended mixed Monday, after gold, silver and the platinum metal group (PGM) all rallied strongly early, but the strength of the PGM's would continue to provide support for the rest of the complex, analysts said.

"Gold ran up early on fund shortcovering and silver was dragged along, helped by the dollar sliding further against most currencies, but the rally ran into some profit taking by locals and the trade," said Pioneer Futures senior analyst Scott Meyers in New York.
"I don't think gold and silver are going to fall apart from here, but it maybe a case of waiting to buy the dip now, while the platinum/gold spread provides support," he said."
COMEX June gold ended down 60 cents at $348.70 an ounce, but not before climbing to its highest intraday level since April 8 at $352.20.

The move back above $350 in June gold was forcing more fund shortcovering, analysts said, after COMEX gold open interest fell a further 990 lots Friday to 163,358 contracts, reflecting liquidation by funds last week.

The latest CFTC Commitment of Traders data, released late Friday, showed funds were heavily net short by 40,009 lots as of May 6, compared to a net short position of 37,500 contracts two weeks earlier.

But, after seeing a four year low around $337.00 in January, spot gold prices have found support again in the past few weeks around $340 an ounce, suggesting the low for year may be already in, analysts said.

Spot gold ended quoted $347.40/90 an ounce, after seeing an intraday high around $350.90, compared to the New York close Friday around $347.80/30. In London gold fixed at $348.20 Monday afternoon, the highest fix for a month.
The main change in economic fundamentals recently has been the sudden sharp slide in the U.S. dollar, analysts said.

After seeing four year highs earlier this year, the U.S. dollar slide to new three month lows against the yen early Monday around 116.00 yen, making gold and other precious metals cheaper in yen terms.
In the past year, the strength of the dollar had been one of the factors behind gold's weakness, with Japanese gold demand slumping by nearly 50 percent, according to the World Gold Council.
Robust physical offtake in India is also providing support, with the Indian wedding season still about a month from winding down.

Another factor improving sentiment Monday was the reported split developing in the Swiss cabinet over whether to proceed with Swiss gold sales to finance the proposed fund to compensate victims of the Holocaust. Swiss Defense Minister Adolf Ogi is opposed to the sale of gold and the plan must still win legislative approval and faces a referendum in 1998.

The threat of further European central bank sales still hangs over the gold market, but EU central banks were unlikely to sell more gold this year, according to South African central bank governor, Chris Stals, Monday.
COMEX July silver, proved more volatile than gold as usual, ending down 4.5 cents at $4.835, after seeing an early high at $4.930, its highest level since early April.
Funds were neutral in silver, holding only a small net long position of 149 lots on May 6, the CFTC data showed, compared with a small net short position of 384 contracts two weeks earlier.

NYMEX July platinum ended up $1.70 an ounce at $391.10, after seeing a session high at $#97.50, its highest level since early March. In London Monday platinum fixed at 395.25 an ounce, the highest since February 28.

NYMEX June palladium, held onto the day's gains though, ending up $7.95 at $171.85, after seeing a new contract high at $172.90. In London Monday fixed at its highest level since April 20, 1995 at $171.75.
"With the dollar/yen down at these levels, the Japanese, who have a voracious appetite for palladium, have been buying all the PGM's that are not nailed down," one PGM dealer said.

The combination of stronger U.S. dollar prices for PGM's plus the slide in the dollar/yen rate, forced heavy shortcovering in palladium futures on the Tokyo Commodities Exchange (TOCOM) Monday. Private investors trading on TOCOM are believed to hold short positions equal to about 50 tonnes of palladium.

Meanwhile, the disruption of Russian exports of PGMs since last December has forced PGM dealers to borrow the metals to meet forward sales commitments, pushing up short term lease rates and tipping the market into a rare backwardation.
Russian supplies are expected to resume in June, after the decree authorizing PGM export quotas was signed last week, but analysts fear Russia's marketing strategy may be changing.
"The disaster of the early 1990's when we dumped metal and prices crashed are over," Mikhail Steklov, the director of Norilsk Nickel, said Monday. "We won't do it again."
Norilsk sits on 55 percent of the world's palladium reserves and 20 percent of its platinum reserves.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
